newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldovan government quits after presidential vote.
newsitem.headline: Moldovan government quits after presidential vote.

text.p: Moldova's parliament accepted the resignation of Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli's government on Tuesday, but asked ministers to work on until Petru Lucinschi, who was elected president on Sunday, had formed a new cabinet.
"The government has failed to...achieve economic growth and ensure the social welfare of the population," Sangheli told the deputies. "Under the circumstances, we tender our resignation."

Sangheli, who was knocked out in the first round of the presidential election on November 17, had repeatedly said the government would resign after last Sunday's run-off between Lucinschi and President Mircea Snegur "to preserve civil peace".
"I think the premier and the government have reached a just decision," said Lucinschi from the parliamentary speaker's chair which he has occupied for the past three years.
"But I ask all the members of the cabinet to work hard until a new government is formed," the president-elect added.

Lucinschi, Moldova's former Soviet-era leader and once a senior Communist party official in Moscow, will nominate a new government after he is sworn in on January 15. Parliament must then endorse the new cabinet for ministers to take office.
Lucinschi, a 56-year-old intellectual, stood as a social democrat seeking stronger welfare guarantees and a slowdown in the rapid free market reforms advocated by Snegur.
He said on Monday the new government was likely to include social democrats, liberals and communists.
The new president has also said he wants to improve relations with Moscow, placing less emphasis on links with Moldovans' ethnic kin in neighbouring Romania.
He also plans to re-integrate the separatist Russian-speaking Dnestr region, which broke away in 1990 over fears of Romanian domination.
Snegur and Sangheli had long been at loggerheads, partially paralysing policy-making when Moldova is still deep in the economic crisis that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Last March, the president and prime minister fell out over Snegur's bid to sack the defence minister, creating a split in the army. The constitutional court told Snegur to back down.
